title: Overview & Vision
description: AI-assisted game development with code and content you can own.
content:
# Overview & Vision

Automata is a TypeScript game framework for modern web browsers and Ruken, the reference gaming host.

Automata is designed for developers using coding agents: agents write code and tests; people direct the game and author its content. Start with a working example, make a bounded change, and review the result.

## License

> [!NOTE]
> Framework code is MIT licensed. Third-party dependencies and example artwork retain their own stated terms. See the repository license and asset provenance before redistributing assets.

## Ownership

Only simulation systems change gameplay state during a run. Input sends commands. PixiJS reads render deltas. Effect manages resources and side effects outside the simulation.

## Current starting point

Explore the 2D starter and focused examples before adding your own systems. The Last Light and FloorFifty are reference projects that informed the architecture.

## Packages

| Package | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| @mcthaydt/automata-sim | Simulation, definitions, snapshots and RNG |
| @mcthaydt/automata-runtime | Boot, flow and scoped runtime |
| @mcthaydt/automata-render-pixi | PixiJS presentation |
| @mcthaydt/automata-ui | Responsive geometry and UI |
| @mcthaydt/automata-host | Hosting sessions |
| @mcthaydt/automata-content | Content validation and compilation |

title: Quick Start
description: Play a double-jump remix, copy a task, and run the starter on your machine.
content:
# Quick Start

## Play before setup

[Try the double-jump remix](/start#worked-change) in your browser. Jump, release, and press again before landing. Toggle the extra jump off to compare the original. The same page includes the prompt, source, and tests.

## Run the starter locally

Use Node 24.21.0 or newer and pnpm 10.34.6.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/mcthaydt/automata-framework.git
cd automata-framework
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm --filter @af-examples/base-2d dev
```

Open the URL printed by Vite and play Emberwick. The starter is a working TypeScript browser game that you can edit directly or with a coding agent.

## Give your agent one idea

[Copy the double-jump task](/start#first-task). It adds one extra jump through a plugin, reuses the existing player input and movement definitions, and tests held input, landing, and snapshots. [Install agent skills](/docs/agent-setup) for the guided workflow when you set up your agent.

A configurable player start is also included as a smaller content exercise. Its helper uses parseRoom to validate the new room while keeping the source content unchanged.

## Check and play the result

```sh
pnpm --filter @af-examples/base-2d check
pnpm --filter @af-examples/base-2d build
```

Try the new behavior and the original controls yourself. Ask the agent to report the files changed, the checks it ran, and any browser or device behavior it has not verified.

## Choose your next change

[Choose a task prompt](/ai#task-prompts) for a collectible, dash, jump feedback, room content, saves, or release preparation. The [API reference](/cheatsheet) provides examples and current package entry points.

## License and scope

Framework code is MIT licensed; assets and third-party dependencies retain their own terms. Browser and mobile foundations are available. Networking and server packages remain planned. See [capabilities and licensing](/docs/capabilities).

title: From Unity
description: Map GameObjects, MonoBehaviours, scenes and ScriptableObjects to Automata ownership.
content:
# From Unity

Keep the habit of composing a game from small pieces. In Automata, separate the data that determines gameplay from the objects that draw it.

## Map familiar concepts

| Your starting point | Automata responsibility |
|---|---|
| GameObject and gameplay components | A simulation entity with data components; its PixiJS view is separate. |
| FixedUpdate gameplay rules | Synchronous systems running in fixed simulation ticks. |
| Update and visual feedback | Presentation and input outside the simulation; drawing can happen between ticks. |
| Scenes, prefabs and ScriptableObjects | Authored content plus explicit spawning and setup code. There is no scene or prefab importer. |
| Editor inspector tweaks | Edit typed content or tuning values and verify the result with tests and the playable example. |

## The habit to change

Avoid making each view object responsible for its own gameplay state. Send input as commands and let simulation systems own the resulting state.

## Your first small port

Start by moving P in Emberwick’s room content. Read room.test.ts, then follow player-move.system.ts and play-room.ts to see how content, rules and drawing connect.

[Open Emberwick’s source](/examples?demo=base-2d) and [try the worked change](/start#worked-change).

## Compatibility and scope

Unity APIs, packages, serialized scenes and editor tooling are not drop-in dependencies. Port one mechanic first rather than translating a whole project.

[Current capabilities](/docs/capabilities).

title: From Godot
description: Map nodes, scenes, signals, resources and physics callbacks to simulation and presentation.
content:
# From Godot

A Godot scene tree combines several responsibilities. In Automata, identify which parts describe gameplay state, which parts draw it, and which parts manage input or resources.

## Map familiar concepts

| Your starting point | Automata responsibility |
|---|---|
| Nodes and scenes | Entities and data for gameplay, with separate PixiJS containers or HTML/Svelte UI for presentation. |
| _physics_process gameplay logic | Fixed-tick simulation systems. |
| _process visual updates | Presentation outside the simulation, including drawing between ticks. |
| Signals | Explicit commands and events at ownership boundaries; do not assume a global signal replacement. |
| Resources and exported properties | Typed content and tuning data, validated by the project’s parsers and schemas. |

## The habit to change

Keep the scene graph as a presentation structure. Do not turn it into a second owner of gameplay state.

## Your first small port

Read the room content and its validation tests, then trace input through play-room.ts into the movement system. Rebuild one small scene interaction as a command and system.

[Open Emberwick’s source](/examples?demo=base-2d) and [try the worked change](/start#worked-change).

## Compatibility and scope

There is no .tscn, GDScript or resource converter. Preserve the behavior you need, then implement it using Automata’s current APIs.

[Current capabilities](/docs/capabilities).

title: From Unreal
description: Map Actors, components, Blueprints and replication expectations to the current 2D framework.
content:
# From Unreal

Bring the habit of defining ownership and boundaries, but evaluate the current 2D browser toolchain before planning a port from a full Unreal project.

## Map familiar concepts

| Your starting point | Automata responsibility |
|---|---|
| Actors and gameplay components | Simulation entities with data components and systems; rendering is a separate view. |
| Blueprint gameplay graphs | Reviewable TypeScript systems, commands and tests. Automata has no Blueprint editor. |
| Tick | Fixed simulation ticks for rules and a separate frame loop for drawing. |
| Levels and data assets | Authored content and explicit project setup. |
| Replication and server authority | A roadmap concern: networking and server packages are planned, not a replacement for Unreal replication today. |

## The habit to change

Make the server/networking requirement an explicit capability check. A deterministic simulation alone does not supply transport, matchmaking or replication.

## Your first small port

Try the browser starter and the fixed-step loop tests. Port one self-contained 2D mechanic with a clear command, state change and test before considering a larger project.

[Open Emberwick’s source](/examples?demo=base-2d) and [try the worked change](/start#worked-change).

## Compatibility and scope

Do not choose the current framework as a drop-in replacement for Unreal’s 3D renderer, editor, asset pipeline or networking stack.

[Current capabilities](/docs/capabilities).

title: From GameMaker
description: Map objects, instances, events, rooms and alarms to data, systems and content.
content:
# From GameMaker

The room and event model is a useful starting vocabulary. The main change is to make gameplay state explicit and keep drawing separate from rules.

## Map familiar concepts

| Your starting point | Automata responsibility |
|---|---|
| Objects and instances | Entities carrying data components, created through explicit setup. |
| Create events | Entity initialization and plugin/project setup. |
| Step events | Systems that advance gameplay in fixed ticks. |
| Draw and Draw GUI events | PixiJS presentation and game UI outside the simulation. |
| Rooms and alarms | Authored room content and tick-based state for timed gameplay. Keep wall-clock timers outside the sim. |

## The habit to change

Avoid coupling a drawing instance to the only copy of gameplay state. Keep rules in systems and let views observe the result.

## Your first small port

Open room.ts and map #, ., P and G to the playable room. Make one content edit, run the room tests, then inspect the movement system as the equivalent of a focused Step rule.

[Open Emberwick’s source](/examples?demo=base-2d) and [try the worked change](/start#worked-change).

## Compatibility and scope

Automata does not import .yy projects or execute GML. Rebuild a small room or mechanic first and retain your original project as the behavior reference.

[Current capabilities](/docs/capabilities).

title: From web development
description: Map application state, components, requestAnimationFrame and async work to game ownership.
content:
# From web development

TypeScript, Vite and browser tools will be familiar. The new discipline is to give simulation time and gameplay state explicit owners rather than updating them from every UI callback.

## Map familiar concepts

| Your starting point | Automata responsibility |
|---|---|
| Application state | Gameplay state belongs to the simulation; menus and UI can still own their own UI state. |
| UI components and DOM | Svelte/HTML UI or PixiJS presentation. Simulation components are data, not UI components. |
| requestAnimationFrame | Drive drawing per frame; advance game rules through the fixed-step loop. |
| Click/key callbacks | Translate input into commands instead of mutating gameplay entities from the view. |
| fetch, timers and cleanup effects | Resource work outside the simulation, with Effect-managed lifetimes where the runtime owns it. |

## The habit to change

Keep Date, Math.random, network requests and DOM access out of simulation steps. Use the framework’s deterministic inputs, time and RNG where gameplay depends on them.

## Your first small port

Read loop.ts and loop.test.ts, then trace play-room.ts from input to sim.step and renderer.draw. Make the configurable-start change before adding a new mechanic.

[Open Emberwick’s source](/examples?demo=base-2d) and [try the worked change](/start#worked-change).

## Compatibility and scope

A game loop is not a component rerender loop. Browser and device performance still require measurement, even when the source looks like a familiar web application.

[Current capabilities](/docs/capabilities).

title: ECS Simulation & Determinism
description: Components, systems, async creation and synchronous stepping.
content:
# ECS Simulation & Determinism

## Definitions

Use defineComponent for fields, defineSystem for a synchronous run function, and definePlugin to register components and systems. Systems query entities through SimContext and write through entity.set.

## Creation and ticks

Await createSim with a seed and plugins. Creation can initialize plugin engines asynchronously. Once created, sim.step(commands) advances one fixed tick synchronously. The default tick rate is 60 Hz.

## Repeatable runs

Keep I/O, wall-clock time, Math.random, DOM and Effect outside simulation steps. Use context RNG streams and the framework's deterministic math where required. Replay equivalence depends on matching code, content, initial state and commands; use the cross-engine checks for evidence.

## Snapshots and lifetime

Use sim.snapshot() to serialize state and sim.restore(bytes) to restore a compatible snapshot. Call sim.dispose() when the simulation is no longer needed.

title: PixiJS 2D Presentation
description: Renderer setup, render deltas and interpolation.
content:
# PixiJS 2D Presentation

## Renderer setup

Import @mcthaydt/automata-render-pixi/no-eval before initializing PixiJS. createPixiRenderer returns a factory that accepts the runtime render target and produces a scoped Effect.

WebGL2 is the default. WebGPU is opt-in. Test the renderer you plan to ship on the devices you support.

## Between ticks

Presentation reads render deltas instead of changing gameplay state. Interpolate between previous and current values when drawing between simulation ticks.

```ts
sprite.x = previous.x + (current.x - previous.x) * alpha
```

## Working examples

The renderer example demonstrates presentation in isolation. Emberwick adds a playable room. Use those sources for the complete boot and disposal flow.

title: Effect Runtime & Concurrency
description: Loading, errors and resource lifetimes outside the sim.
content:
# Effect Runtime & Concurrency

## Boot

runGame accepts a GameDefinition and returns a RuntimeHandle. It owns boot attempts, resources and shutdown. Use the runtime package types for the full definition.

## Resource ownership

Effect scopes manage resource lifetimes outside the simulation. Keep file and network access, loading, timers and persistent saves out of simulation systems.

## Failure and recovery

Boot failures are typed. Inspect the runtime example for its loading, retry and failure behavior. A typed boundary makes failure explicit; it does not guarantee a game cannot crash.

title: Zero-Eval CSP & Ruken Security
description: Avoiding dynamic evaluation under the host policy.
content:
# Zero-Eval CSP & Ruken Security

## Dynamic evaluation

Do not use eval or new Function in game code. Ruken does not permit unsafe-eval. Import the renderer's no-eval entry before initializing PixiJS.

## Policy scope

Avoiding dynamic evaluation is one part of CSP compatibility. Asset origins, connections, workers and other directives must also match the host policy. Test the built game under that actual policy: a Ruken game's headers come from compileHeaders in @ruken/manifest, and the framework CLI's CSP probe loads the build in Chromium under them. See [the content security policy](/ai#csp).

## Trust boundaries

Keep credentials outside game bundles. Validate host messages at the integration boundary. Use the supported hosting API instead of inventing another handshake.

title: Mobile UI Primitives
content:
# Mobile UI Primitives

## Geometry

createGeometryOwner tracks the space available to game UI, including host geometry and viewport changes. Use its state instead of independent measurements in every component.

## Layout and controls

ScreenFrame, ActionBar, CornerControls and Dialog provide building blocks. Check their current Props definitions rather than guessing component inputs.

## Device checks

Verify touch targets, focus order, orientation changes, safe areas and keyboard occlusion on supported devices. A responsive layout test does not establish GPU performance or real-device acceptance.

## Tested input journeys

At 780×270, the framework’s input matrix plays a touch journey and a gamepad journey in Chromium under a fake Ruken host. Keyboard journeys run at the tablet and desktop sizes, in Chromium, WebKit and Firefox at desktop size. These are browser tests with simulated input and DOM geometry. Acceptance on real phones and controllers is separate and still open. [Read the matrix](https://github.com/mcthaydt/automata-framework/blob/f8023a907725cccd84277372c0d4f1b73d2da90c/packages/testing/src/e2e/input-matrix.ts) at the framework commit this site was built from.

title: AI Coding Agent Rules
description: Project context for agents, followed by verification.
content:
# AI Coding Agent Rules

## Start from source

Install Superpowers and the official PixiJS v8 skills, then have the agent report which guidance it loaded. See [Install agent skills](/docs/agent-setup). Give the agent AGENTS.md, current package types and the nearest working example. Read instructions through the agent's supported project-context mechanism.

## Boundaries

- Only simulation systems mutate gameplay state during a run.
- Effect runs outside the sim.
- Avoid dynamic evaluation; verify the actual host CSP.
- Presentation interpolates between ticks and observes render deltas.
- Report the checks performed and the gates still open.

## Verify the result

Instructions cannot eliminate hallucinations or guarantee correct code. Check exported names, typecheck changes, run relevant tests and inspect runtime behavior.

## Plain-text context

The website publishes llms.txt as an index; llms-full.txt, the framework's defined documentation corpus followed by its complete API reference, and llms-api.txt, that reference alone, both generated from the package declarations by the framework's API index; and llms-guides.txt, this site's guides and task prompts. None of them is the framework source.

title: Capabilities and licensing
description: What you can use today, what is planned, and how the license applies.
content:
# Capabilities and licensing

## Available foundations

- Browser games with a playable 2D starter and standalone delivery.
- Phone-first interface primitives, keyboard and touch input examples.
- Simulation systems, seeded randomness, snapshots and replays.
- Explicit source files and tests that people and coding agents can inspect and change.

## Planned

Multiplayer networking and server packages are planned. Deterministic simulation and replays are foundations for that work, not a complete multiplayer service. Full 3D support and further gameplay extensions follow the framework roadmap.

## MIT framework code

The framework code uses the MIT license. You may use it in commercial games and modify it without publishing your game's source, subject to retaining the required license notice. Read the repository's LICENSE for the full terms.

## Assets and extensions

The framework license does not replace third-party dependency licenses or asset-specific terms. Example art has provenance files in its project; fonts have their own licenses. Any extension sold under separate terms must state those terms explicitly.

title: Boot errors
description: The typed failures boot reports, generated from the framework API index.
content:
# Boot errors

Every way boot can fail; each draws on the runtime's boot failure panel (shared contracts §4).

```ts
type BootError = HostError | ContentHashMismatch | AssetLoadFailed | LoadStalled | RendererUnavailable | BootDefect;
```

These are the failures boot reports as typed values. A defect in game code after boot is not one of them, and this list is not a claim that every failure is caught. [Read the source](https://github.com/mcthaydt/automata-framework/blob/f8023a907725cccd84277372c0d4f1b73d2da90c/packages/runtime/src/boot/boot-error.ts) at the framework commit this site was built from.

## The failures

### HostError

From `@mcthaydt/automata-host`. Any failure after the handshake. A request that fails never falls back to another path.

### ContentHashMismatch

From `@mcthaydt/automata-runtime`. Content hash does not match expected hash.

### AssetLoadFailed

From `@mcthaydt/automata-runtime`. An asset download failed with a non-OK HTTP status or network error (status 0).

### LoadStalled

From `@mcthaydt/automata-runtime`. A resource download had no progress reported for STALL_MS (30 s).
Triggers the "Taking a while" screen with a Try again button.

### RendererUnavailable

From `@mcthaydt/automata-runtime`. Neither WebGL2 nor WebGPU could be initialized.
In Ruken this presents the "unsupported" screen with an exit button.

### BootDefect

From `@mcthaydt/automata-runtime`. An unexpected defect during boot.

title: Install agent skills
description: Install Superpowers and the official PixiJS collection, then verify the agent can load them.
content:
# Install agent skills

## Required for the guided AI workflow

Install Superpowers and the official PixiJS v8 skill collection for the agent you will use. They guide planning, testing and rendering work; they are not runtime dependencies of the game.

## Install Superpowers

In the Codex app, open Plugins and install Superpowers. In Codex CLI, use /plugins, search for Superpowers and select Install Plugin.

In Claude Code, use its official plugin marketplace:

```text
/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official
```

In Cursor Agent chat:

```text
/add-plugin superpowers
```

Other agents have their own installation routes. Use the [upstream Superpowers instructions](https://github.com/obra/superpowers#installation).

## Install PixiJS skills

Run this in the checkout and follow the prompts for your coding agent and the full PixiJS collection:

```sh
npx skills add https://github.com/pixijs/pixijs-skills
```

See the [official PixiJS instructions](https://github.com/pixijs/pixijs-skills#installing).

## Verify before coding

Ask the agent to confirm installed and loaded skills, rather than inferring readiness from a website checkbox.

```text
Before coding, check the skills available in this agent session.
Confirm Superpowers is installed, including using-superpowers and its planning/testing workflows.
Confirm the official PixiJS v8 skill collection is installed, including the pixijs router and relevant rendering skills.
Read the applicable SKILL.md files and report their loaded paths or plugin names.
If either collection is missing or cannot be loaded, stop and follow its upstream installation instructions before implementing.
Then read this checkout's AGENTS.md and current package types. Project rules take precedence.
Do not report a skill as installed or loaded without evidence.
```

[Use the interactive setup checklist](/start). Installation sources were checked on 15 October 2026; follow upstream instructions when a tool changes.

title: Who Automata is for
description: Choose Automata based on your workflow and current requirements.
content:
# Who Automata is for

## Who this is for

- You build with coding agents and want source files and tests you can inspect.
- You are making a 2D browser game and want phone-first interface foundations.
- You want people to own the art, rooms, rules and creative direction.
- You are willing to work in TypeScript, review changes and keep tests with the game.

## Who this is not for

- You need a visual scene editor or drag-and-drop game-making workflow.
- You need a complete 3D engine, editor tooling or Unreal-style rendering pipeline today.
- You need production-ready multiplayer networking and server packages out of the box.
- You expect a finished game from one prompt without reviewing code or testing the result.

## Start from your background

- [From Unity](/docs/from-unity)
- [From Godot](/docs/from-godot)
- [From Unreal](/docs/from-unreal)
- [From GameMaker](/docs/from-gamemaker)
- [From web development](/docs/from-web)

[Current capabilities and licensing](/docs/capabilities).

title: FAQ
description: Answers about agents, content, licensing, platforms, migration and community games.
content:
# FAQ

## Do I need to know how to code?

You should be willing to read and change TypeScript, or learn it alongside your agent. Automata makes ownership explicit, but it does not turn game development into a no-code workflow.

## Do I have to use AI?

No. The framework is ordinary source code that you can edit and test yourself. The guided workflow is designed for coding agents, with human review and creative control.

## Which skills should my agent have?

Install Superpowers and the official PixiJS v8 skill collection for the agent you are actually using. Then ask it to report the available skills and load the relevant guidance. These are requirements for the recommended AI workflow, not runtime dependencies of your game.

## Which coding agents can I use?

Use an agent that can read the checkout, edit files and run tests. Installation differs between Codex, Claude Code, Cursor and other tools; the agent setup guide links the current upstream instructions.

## Can I sell a game built with Automata?

The framework code is MIT licensed, which permits commercial use under the license terms without requiring publication of your game source. Keep required notices and check separate asset, dependency, extension and tool terms.

## Can I make the content myself?

Yes. Edit room data, art, rules and narrative directly. The worked example lets you choose a starting position while reusing the existing simulation and renderer. You can also edit any of the code yourself.

## Does it run in browsers and on phones?

Browser delivery and phone-first UI foundations are available, with keyboard and touch examples. Test your own game on the devices, orientations and browsers you intend to support.

## Is multiplayer ready?

Networking and server packages are planned. Deterministic state, snapshots and replays provide foundations for that work; they are not a complete multiplayer service.

## Does it support full 3D today?

The current public starting point is 2D. Further rendering and full 3D work are on the roadmap. Choose based on current capability status rather than planned features.

## Can I import an existing engine project?

There is no automatic Unity, Godot, Unreal or GameMaker project converter. The migration guides map familiar concepts and recommend rebuilding one small mechanic first.

## How does it help a game grow beyond a prototype?

Explicit state ownership, separate systems and packages, and repeatable tests help keep changes bounded as the project grows. They do not promise a particular player count or performance level; measure your own game.

## What is Ruken?

Ruken is the reference gaming host integrated by the framework. The starter can also run standalone in a browser; see hosting guidance when adding platform services.

## How do I get my game into the showcase?

Use the community showcase submission link. Include a public playable URL, your creator name, a short description, the Automata version and screenshots you have permission to share. Submissions are reviewed before publication.

[Install agent skills](/docs/agent-setup), [make a first change](/start), or [visit the community showcase](/showcase).
